title: Time, days and dates
description: Tell the time, name the days, and talk about yesterday, today, tomorrow, last week and next week.

guide.title: Clock time
guide.text:
ಗಂಟೆ (gante) means 'hour', 'o'clock' and 'bell'. 'What time is it?' is gante eshtaaytu? - literally 'how much has the hour become?'. The answer puts the number first: aidu gante aaytu, or just aidu gante, 'five o'clock'.

'At five o'clock' adds the dative: ಐದು ಗಂಟೆಗೆ (aidu gantege). 'At what time?' is ಎಷ್ಟು ಗಂಟೆಗೆ? (eshtu gantege?).

Half past is the number + -ವರೆ (-vare), with the final u of the number lengthened: ಐದೂವರೆ (aidoovare) half past five; ಏಳೂವರೆ (eloovare) half past seven; ಹತ್ತೂವರೆ (hattoovare) half past ten. Quarter past is the number + ಕಾಲು (kaalu): aidookaalu, 5:15. Quarter to the next hour is said as 'five and three quarters': aidoomukkaalu, 5:45.

Minutes are ನಿಮಿಷ (nimisha): aidu gante hattu nimisha, 5:10. People also read times in English.

Parts of the day: ಬೆಳಿಗ್ಗೆ (beligge) morning; ಮಧ್ಯಾಹ್ನ (madhyaahna) afternoon; ಸಂಜೆ (sanje) evening; ರಾತ್ರಿ (raatri) night. They are used without any ending: sanje barteeni, 'I'll come in the evening'.

guide.title: Days of the week
guide.text:
The days end in ವಾರ (vaara), which on its own means 'week' and also 'day of the week':

ಭಾನುವಾರ (bhaanuvaara) Sunday; ಸೋಮವಾರ (somavaara) Monday; ಮಂಗಳವಾರ (mangalavaara) Tuesday; ಬುಧವಾರ (budhavaara) Wednesday; ಗುರುವಾರ (guruvaara) Thursday; ಶುಕ್ರವಾರ (shukravaara) Friday; ಶನಿವಾರ (shanivaara) Saturday.

'On Monday' needs no ending, or takes -a dina ('day of'): somavaara barteeni, 'I'll come on Monday'.

To ask the day: ivattu yaava vaara? - 'today (is) which weekday?'

guide.title: Yesterday, today, tomorrow
guide.text:
ಮೊನ್ನೆ (monne) the day before yesterday; ನಿನ್ನೆ (ninne) yesterday; ಇವತ್ತು (ivattu) today; ನಾಳೆ (naale) tomorrow; ನಾಡಿದ್ದು (naadiddu) the day after tomorrow.

ivattu is the spoken word; in writing 'today' is ಇಂದು (indu) or ಈ ದಿನ (ee dina).

ಈಗ (eega) now; ಆಮೇಲೆ (aamele) later; ಆಗಲೇ (aagale) already; ಇನ್ನೂ (innoo) still, yet; ಬೇಗ (bega) early, soon; ತಡ (tada) late - though most people say 'let': let aaytu, 'it got late'.

The tense of the verb must match: ninne bande (I came yesterday), naale barteeni (I'll come tomorrow).

examples.english: The day after tomorrow is a holiday.

guide.title: Weeks, months, years and dates
guide.text:
ದಿನ (dina) day; ವಾರ (vaara) week; ತಿಂಗಳು (tingalu) month; ವರ್ಷ (varsha) year.

'Last' is ಹೋದ (hoda, 'that went') or ಕಳೆದ (kaleda); 'next' is ಮುಂದಿನ (mundina) or ಬರೋ (baro, 'that is coming'); 'this' is ಈ (ee): hoda vaara (last week), ee vaara (this week), mundina vaara (next week), hoda varsha (last year), mundina tingalu (next month).

A length of time takes no ending: eradu dina (for two days), mooru varsha (for three years). 'Ago' is ಹಿಂದೆ (hinde, 'behind') after the possessive form of the time: eradu dinada hinde, 'two days ago'. 'In / after two days' is eradu dinadalli or eradu dina aada mele.

For calendar dates, everyday Kannada uses the English month names with ತಾರೀಖು (taareekhu), 'date': aidane taareekhu, 'the fifth'. Ordinals add -ane to the number: ondane (first), eradane (second), moorane (third), aidane (fifth). 'First' is also ಮೊದಲನೇ (modalane).

phrases.note: 'taim eshtaaytu?' (ಟೈಮ್ ಎಷ್ಟಾಯ್ತು?) is just as common.
elu + vare; the first e is long.
The o of soma is long.

phrases.english: What day of the week is it today?

phrases.note: Spoken form; in writing it is baruttene (ಬರುತ್ತೇನೆ).

phrases.english: The day after tomorrow is a holiday.
Last week I was in my home town.

phrases.note: horadu = to set out. Written: horaduttade (ಹೊರಡುತ್ತದೆ).

phrases.english: I don't have time right now.
